t: The 4 Cornerstones Of Smart Classroom Management nagement/
q: These principles, or cornerstones, form the heart of what we believe to be the solution to the scores of behavior-related challenges facing teachers today.
Any method or strategy that causes friction with students will always make classroom management more difficult.
It creates resentment and animosity. It causes students to secretly dislike you and misbehave behind your back.
All students—difficult, shy, and confident alike—are drawn to teachers who exude a calm, friendly demeanor.
It is the love of school that is the ultimate reward, the ultimate intrinsic motivator, and the ultimate antidote to unwanted behavior.
Allowing your classroom management plan to be the lone source of accountability removes the need to rely on hurtful and less effective methods of managing behavior.
We offer one unified approach, where every strategy works together harmoniously to craft the optimum teaching and learning environment.

t: Why You Should Let Poorly Followed Routines Play Out s-play-out/
q: Upon noticing a class routine going off the rails, they immediately jump in to try and correct it.
It’s far better to take a step back and let the routine play out.
The only way to fix a sloppy routine so that it doesn’t happen again is to know precisely what went wrong.

When students know they’re being watched intently, especially by a teacher who faithfully holds them accountable for previously learned expectations, they develop the ability to recognize and correct their own mistakes.
When you jump in right away, on the other hand, they’re likely to become defensive, argumentative, and annoyed by your interruption.
Handling misbehavior with patience and composure, on the other hand, will calm and settle your students and refocus them on the task at hand.
Only then will your students begin looking inward at themselves and their responsibilities.

t: How A Simple Change In Thinking Can Improve Behavior ve-behavior/
q: One of the reasons difficult students misbehave is because their teacher expects that they will.
To combat this phenomenon, you must do the opposite. You must assume henceforth that your most challenging students will, of their own accord, behave . . . perfectly.
That isn’t to say that you’ll become lax in your supervision, ignore their misbehavior, or in any way become less consistent holding them accountable.
This simple change in thinking—in how you choose to see them—effectively removes an infinite number of verbal and non-verbal signals that reinforce their poor behavior.
It upends their attitude toward you, transforming them from someone who firmly believes that you’re out to get them . . . into your biggest fan.
They’ll see in your eyes a reflection of themselves they may not at first recognize, but who deep down they’ve always wanted to be.

t: Why You Must Remind Students Of Their Purpose https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2014/07/05/why-you-must-remind-students-of-their-purpose/
q: If not reminded, and reminded often, your students will naturally slip into believing that school is just something they’re supposed to do.
This attitude can cause students to take their education for granted, to see it as a grind, as something they’re forced to do rather than what it is.
Doing anything begrudgingly, anything with the specter of having to do it hanging over your head, can be a dangerous thing.
It is the ‘why’ of school, after all, that cracks ajar the gates of learning.
You tell them. You tell them every day why they’re there, why what they’re doing is important, and why what you have to offer them is a most precious gift.
Coming from someone your students like and admire, and delivered with passion, this simple message—which will vary in depth depending on grade level—can be powerful and deeply impressionable.
